en: It is twelve past three in the morning.
Your phone buzzes: SLO fast burn.
Is it the nightly update again, or is the disk really full this time?
Paeon sits next to your alerting.
It listens to OpenObserve, uptime-kuma, and anything that speaks the Alertmanager webhook.
It groups alerts into incidents.
A cheap model triages: noise, transient, a known issue, or real?
A strong model investigates, with tools that can only read.
You get a root cause, the evidence, and a plan.
A hard line separates what a model may think from what code may do.
No shell, no free-form command, no write credential for a model, in any stage.
The core reads attacker-controlled text, and talks to models.
The executor holds the one write credential, and believes only its own copy of the rules and a link you tapped.
The catalog is closed: six actions exist.
The rules file switches them on for targets you name. It cannot add one.
A configuration change is never applied: it opens a pull request.
Go or No-go arrives on your phone.
The button is signed, single-use, expiring, and bound to the exact plan.
Opening the link never applies anything.
Everything is an event in one append-only log: every alert, decision, model call with its cost, and tool result.
Budgets per incident and per day, and a storm guard per hour.
A spent budget never hides an alert: Paeon fails open.
Allow-lists first, redaction second.
Out of the box, Paeon takes no action on your server: acting is a second process you add on purpose.
It is alpha software: the acting part has not yet run on a real server for long.
Run it next to your alerting, never instead of it.
Small: one container, one SQLite file, one YAML file.
Models think. You say Go. Code does.
